title: Within- and Between-Group Correlation Methods
text: method = "sem" fits two-level structural equation model using lavaan::sem(), grouping variable cluster variable. Rather decomposing observed scores correlating resulting deviation scores group means, method estimates within-group -group covariance matrices directly simultaneously, using robust maximum likelihood (MLR; Hox, Moerbeek, & van de Schoot, 2018, ch. 14, sec. 14.3). standardized solution provides within- -group correlations, significance based resulting z-tests. MLR estimation incorporates group’s sample size likelihood automatically, separate weight argument method: unequal group sizes handled natively estimation procedure , rather explicit weighting choice. Missing data handled listwise deletion (cases missing value modeled variables excluded estimation). Variables never vary within group (e.g., stable trait measured per person attached every observation) contribute within-group covariance modeled -group level; variables intraclass correlation near zero modeled within-group level. Correlations estimated given level reported NA.

title: Getting Started with mlstats
text: demonstrate, use media_diary, simulated daily diary dataset included mlstats. mimics study 100 participants completed brief daily surveys 14 consecutive days (N = 100 persons, T = 1,400 daily observations). variables : person: person identifier self_control: trait self-control, measured study entry (stable, -person characteristic; ICC ≈ 1) wellbeing: daily positive wellbeing (1–7) screen_time: minutes entertainment media consumed day stress: daily perceived stress (1–7) enjoyment: enjoyment media watched day (1–7) data long format: row one diary entry (one person one day). person column identifies person row belongs .

title: Getting Started with mlstats
text: mldesc() produces publication-ready descriptive statistics table combines means, standard deviations, ranges, ICCs, within-/-group correlation matrix single object:
code: vars <- c("self_control", "wellbeing", "screen_time", "stress")  result <- mldesc(   data  = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars  = vars )  result #> # Multilevel Descriptive Statistics #>   ============ ===== ====== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== #>   variable     n_obs      m    sd range   `1`   `2`   `3`   `4`   icc #>   ------------ ----- ------ ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- #> 1 Self control 1,400   4.03  0.83   2–6     –    NA    NA    NA  1.00 #> 2 Wellbeing    1,400   4.45  0.87   2–7  .61*     –  .42* -.43*   .46 #> 3 Screen time  1,400 128.66 42.29 0–272 -.67* -.34*     –  .29*   .45 #> 4 Stress       1,400   3.81  0.91   1–7 -.53* -.38*  .38*     –   .33 #>   ============ ===== ====== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== #> # ℹ Within-person correlations above, between-person correlations below the #> #   diagonal. #> # ℹ All correlations marked with a star are significant at p < .05. #> # ℹ Correlations estimated via variance decomposition. #> # ℹ Group-weighted multilevel descriptive statistics computed with mlstats.

title: Getting Started with mlstats
text: Three estimation methods available via method argument: method = "decomposition" (default): Uses variance-decomposition approach estimate within- -group correlations. -group correlations descriptive statistics weighted group size weight = TRUE (default). Set weight = FALSE give every group equal influence. method = "sem": Fits two-level structural equation model via lavaan using robust maximum likelihood. handles unequal group sizes rigorously. method = "bayes": Fits Bayesian multilevel models via brms, reporting credible intervals instead p-values. Requires additional ci folder arguments; see vignette("multilevel-descriptives"). See vignette("correlation-methods") detailed comparison.

title: Getting Started with mlstats
text: Several options control appearance output: significance = "detailed": Adds stars p < .05, p < .01, p < .001. default ("basic") marks p < .05. flip = TRUE: Swaps correlation matrix (, within ). remove_leading_zero = FALSE: Keeps leading zero decimal numbers. default removes APA formatting (.45 instead 0.45).

what: Decomposing Variables into Within- and Between-Person Components
title: Getting Started with mlstats
text: fitting multilevel models, time-varying predictors typically decomposed within-group -group components. decompose_within_between() makes easy adding, default, two new columns per variable: _between_{group}: group mean (stable -group component) _within_{group}: deviation group mean (within-group fluctuation) third, optional column can requested via components: _grand_mean_centered: grand-mean-centered value within components serve separate predictors Random Effects Within-(REWB) models, estimate distinct within-group -group effects. title: Multilevel Descriptive Statistics
text: within_between_correlations() returns single correlation matrix within-group correlations appear diagonal -group correlations appear . example dataset, observations nested within persons, function computes within-person correlations (upper triangle) -person correlations (lower triangle).
code: within_between_correlations(   data  = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars  = vars ) #> # Within- and Between-Person Correlations #>   ============ ====== ====== ===== ====== #>   variable        `1`    `2`   `3`    `4` #>   ------------ ------ ------ ----- ------ #> 1 self_control      –     NA    NA     NA #> 2 wellbeing     0.61*      – 0.42* -0.43* #> 3 screen_time  -0.67* -0.34*     –  0.29* #> 4 stress       -0.53* -0.38* 0.38*      – #>   ============ ====== ====== ===== ====== #> # ℹ Within-person correlations above, between-person correlations below the #> #   diagonal. #> # ℹ All correlations marked with a star are significant at p < .05. #> # ℹ Correlations estimated via variance decomposition.

title: Multilevel Descriptive Statistics
text: Upper triangle — within-person correlations: coefficient answers: given person, days score higher average variable X, also tend score higher average variable Y? example, cell stress meets wellbeing upper triangle tells us days higher stress usual also tend days lower wellbeing person. time-invariant variables (e.g., trait self-control), within-group correlations estimated appear NA upper triangle. Lower triangle — -person correlations: coefficient answers: persons score higher variable X average also tend score higher variable Y average? example, cell stress meets wellbeing lower triangle tells us people stressed average also tend worse wellbeing overall.

title: Multilevel Descriptive Statistics
text: Importantly, within-group -group correlations can sometimes differ direction: two correlations screen_time wellbeing tell different stories: Within-person (upper triangle): Positive. days person watches entertainment media typically , wellbeing tends slightly higher average — consistent short-term escapism mood repair. -person (lower triangle): Negative. People watch entertainment media average tend lower average wellbeing — perhaps chronic heavy media use reflects lower trait self-control. Now look naive pooled correlation gives: pooled correlation near zero. researcher relying number conclude entertainment media use relationship wellbeing — missing real positive within-person effect real negative -person association point opposite directions.
code: within_between_correlations(   data  = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars  = c("wellbeing", "screen_time") ) #> # Within- and Between-Person Correlations #>   =========== ====== ===== #>   variable       `1`   `2` #>   ----------- ------ ----- #> 1 wellbeing        – 0.42* #> 2 screen_time -0.34*     – #>   =========== ====== ===== #> # ℹ Within-person correlations above, between-person correlations below the #> #   diagonal. #> # ℹ All correlations marked with a star are significant at p < .05. #> # ℹ Correlations estimated via variance decomposition. cor(media_diary$screen_time, media_diary$wellbeing) #> [1] 0.04597101

title: Multilevel Descriptive Statistics
text: Three estimation methods within- -group correlations available via method argument: method = "decomposition" (default): fast, closed-form variance-decomposition approach (Pedhazur, 1997). Within-group correlations computed group-mean-centred scores; -group correlations computed group means. method = "sem": Fits two-level structural equation model using robust maximum likelihood. handles unequal group sizes rigorously significance testing. method = "bayes": Fits Bayesian multivariate models via brms, reporting credible intervals instead p-values. See vignette("correlation-methods") statistical rationale “Bayesian Estimation” additional arguments requires. weight argument (decomposition method ) controls much influence group -group estimate: weight = TRUE (default): -group correlations descriptive statistics weighted group size. Recommended unbalanced data recover correct population-level estimate (Snijders & Bosker, 2012). weight = FALSE: Every group counts equally regardless size. Note significance tests -group correlations always use unweighted group means regardless weight setting — see vignette("correlation-methods") statistical rationale.
code: within_between_correlations(   data   = media_diary,   group  = "person",   vars   = vars,   method = "sem" # or "bayes" ) within_between_correlations(   data   = media_diary,   group  = "person",   vars   = vars,   weight = FALSE )

title: Multilevel Descriptive Statistics
text: Several options control appearance: significance = "detailed": Adds one star p < .05, two p < .01, three p < .001. default ("basic") marks p < .05. flip = TRUE: Swaps positions within- -person correlations (diagonal, within ). remove_leading_zero = FALSE: Keeps leading zero decimal numbers. default removes APA formatting (.45 instead 0.45). method weight arguments can also used work exactly within_between_correlations() (see ).

text: method = "bayes" (available within_between_correlations() mldesc()) requires brms package, installed mlstats default (install.packages("brms")), two additional arguments: folder: directory fitted brms models cached. title: REWB Models
text: decompose_within_between() splits specified variable three components: _between_{group}: group mean (stable -group component) _within_{group}: deviation group mean (within-group fluctuation) _grand_mean_centered: grand-mean-centered value (opt-; see ) vars argument names variables decompose. group names grouping variable. default, decompose_within_between() returns within- -group components — two predictors REWB models need. screen_time_within_person group-mean-centred score: many (fewer) minutes person watched today compared average. screen_time_between_person person’s average screen time, repeated every row belonging person.

Illustrating interpretation: people watch one minute per day average show 0.0071 lower wellbeing. someone watches 60 minutes per day average another person, expected wellbeing gap 0.43 points. two effects point opposite directions — exactly pattern built simulation. naive regression conflates : naive coefficient near zero positive within-person negative -person effects cancel — entirely uninformative result hides two simulated effects pointing opposite directions. illustrates naive regression can misleading within- -group processes operate simultaneously.

title: Decompose Variables into Within-Group and Between-Group Components — decompose_within_between
text: decomposition commonly used multilevel modeling separate within-group -group variance components (Enders & Tofighi, 2007). decomposed variables particularly useful Random Effects Within-(REWB) models (Bell et al., 2019), allow estimation distinct within-group -group effects. function performs three centering operations: 1. Grand mean centering: value expressed deviation overall sample mean. centers entire distribution zero. 2. -group component: observation, equals mean group. values constant within groups vary groups. REWB models, represents -group effect predictor. 3. Within-group component: value expressed deviation group mean. removes -group variance represents within-group effect predictor REWB models.

title: Compute Multilevel Descriptive Statistics — mldesc
text: data data frame containing variables analyze. group character string specifying name grouping variable. vars character vector specifying names variables describe. method Character string specifying estimation method correlations ICC: "decomposition" (default), "sem", "bayes". See within_between_correlations details correlation methods. method = "bayes", ICC also estimated Bayesian intercept-model (via brms::brm) instead lme4::lmer, reporting posterior median. weight Logical. TRUE (default), mean SD calculated across observations (larger groups contribute ), -group correlation gives weight larger groups. FALSE, every group counts equally: mean SD calculated group means, -group correlation unweighted. correlations, used method = "decomposition" method = "bayes". flip Logical. TRUE, -group correlations shown upper triangle within-group correlations lower triangle. Default FALSE. significance Character string specifying significance marking style. Either "basic" (default) "detailed". "basic", correlations p < .05 marked star. "detailed", correlations marked 1-3 stars p < .05, p < .01, p < .001, respectively. Ignored (message) method = "bayes", always marks correlations whose credible interval excludes zero single star. ci Numeric value strictly 0 1 specifying credible interval width used within-group -group correlations method   = "bayes". Default 0.9 (90% CI). ICC always reports posterior median affected argument. Ignored (message) methods. folder Character string specifying directory path brms models saved. Required method = "bayes"; ignored (message) otherwise. Default NULL. remove_leading_zero Logical. TRUE (default), removes leading zeros decimal values correlation ICC columns according APA standards.

title: Compute Multilevel Descriptive Statistics — mldesc
text: tibble class mlstats_desc_tibble containing: variable: Variable name n_obs: Number observations m: Mean sd: Standard deviation range: Range minimum maximum One column per variable vars containing correlations icc: Intraclass correlation coefficient tibble can returned gt object using print(result, format = "gt") tinytable object using print(result, format = "tt").

title: Compute Multilevel Descriptive Statistics — mldesc
text: function combines three types information: Descriptive statistics: Basic summary statistics variable. weight = TRUE (default), statistics calculated across observations. weight = FALSE, mean mean group means, SD standard deviation group means, representing -group variability. Correlations: Within-group correlations (upper triangle) -group correlations (lower triangle), computed using within_between_correlations. See function's documentation package vignette method estimates correlations tests significance. ICC: intraclass correlation coefficient, computed unconditional (intercept-) multilevel model using lme4::lmer (brms::brm method = "bayes"). ICC represents proportion variance variable lies groups, values close 1 indicating variable barely varies within groups (e.g., stable trait), values close 0 indicating variable barely varies groups (e.g., fast-changing state). ICC always computed linear (Gaussian) model, regardless variable's measurement scale. binary, ordinal, count variables yields linear-probability-style ICC rather latent-scale ICC generalized linear mixed model. warning emitted vars look binary, ordinal, count-like (, whole-number values). method = "bayes", function fits one brms model per variable ICCs, plus models described within_between_correlations correlations — p variables, p ICC fits addition within/-group correlation fits. can take long time larger numbers variables; see vignette("correlation-methods") details.

code: data("media_diary") vars <- c("self_control", "wellbeing", "screen_time", "stress")  # Compute multilevel descriptives (default: decomposition method) result <- mldesc(   data = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars = vars )  result #> # Multilevel Descriptive Statistics #>   ============ ===== ====== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== #>   variable     n_obs      m    sd range   `1`   `2`   `3`   `4`   icc #>   ------------ ----- ------ ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- ----- #> 1 Self control 1,400   4.03  0.83   2–6     –    NA    NA    NA  1.00 #> 2 Wellbeing    1,400   4.45  0.87   2–7  .61*     –  .42* -.43*   .46 #> 3 Screen time  1,400 128.66 42.29 0–272 -.67* -.34*     –  .29*   .45 #> 4 Stress       1,400   3.81  0.91   1–7 -.53* -.38*  .38*     –   .33 #>   ============ ===== ====== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== ===== #> # ℹ Within-person correlations above, between-person correlations below the #> #   diagonal. #> # ℹ All correlations marked with a star are significant at p < .05. #> # ℹ Correlations estimated via variance decomposition. #> # ℹ Group-weighted multilevel descriptive statistics computed with mlstats.  # Compute with unweighted between-group correlations result_unweighted <- mldesc(   data = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars = vars,   weight = FALSE )  # Use SEM-based estimation for correlations (on similarly-scaled variables; # SEM is sensitive to large scale differences, unlike "decomposition") # \donttest{ result_sem <- mldesc(   data = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars = c("self_control", "wellbeing", "stress"),   method = "sem" ) # }  # Use detailed significance marking result_detailed <- mldesc(   data = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars = vars,   significance = "detailed" )  # Use Bayesian estimation for correlations and the ICC (requires brms) # \donttest{ result_bayes <- mldesc(   data = media_diary,   group = "person",   vars = c("self_control", "wellbeing", "screen_time"),   method = "bayes",   folder = tempdir() ) # }

text: data grouping structure (e.g., repeated measurements per person, students nested within schools), single correlation two variables can misleading, mixes two different relationships: variables relate within group (e.g., person's good days also tend productive days?), relate groups (e.g., people generally happier also tend generally productive?). function estimates relationships separately, using one three methods (see Details vignette("correlation-methods") full statistical background).

text: data data frame containing variables analyze. group character string specifying name grouping variable. vars character vector specifying names variables correlate. method Character string specifying estimation method: "decomposition" (default), "sem", "bayes". See Details. weight Logical. Used method = "decomposition" method =   "bayes". TRUE (default), -group correlation gives weight larger groups; significance/credible intervals, however, always based unweighted correlation group means. FALSE, every group counts equally regardless size. Ignored (message) method = "sem", method handles unequal group sizes automatically. flip Logical. TRUE, -group correlations shown upper triangle within-group correlations lower triangle. Default FALSE. significance Character string specifying significance marking style. Either "basic" (default) "detailed". "basic", correlations p < .05 marked star. "detailed", correlations marked 1-3 stars p < .05, p < .01, p < .001, respectively. Ignored (message) method = "bayes", always marks correlations whose credible interval (see ci) excludes zero single star. ci Numeric value strictly 0 1 specifying credible interval width used decide whether correlation starred. applicable method = "bayes"; default 0.9 (90% CI). Ignored (message) methods. folder Character string specifying directory path brms models saved. Required method = "bayes"; ignored (message) otherwise. Default NULL.

title: Compute Within-Group and Between-Group Correlations — within_between_correlations
text: tibble containing correlation matrix : upper triangle contains within-group correlations lower triangle contains -group correlations Diagonal elements marked "–" Significant correlations marked asterisks (see significance parameter, ci method = "bayes") tibble can returned gt object using print(result, format = "gt") tinytable object using print(result, format = "tt").

title: Compute Within-Group and Between-Group Correlations — within_between_correlations
text: Method "decomposition" (default) computes within-group correlation first subtracting group's mean every observation, correlating resulting deviation scores. computes -group correlation correlating group means one another (optionally weighted group size; see weight). approach follows Pedhazur (1997, ch. 16), significance tests account fact subtracting group means uses degrees freedom, following general testing principle Snijders Bosker (2012, sec. 6.1). method fast easy interpret, works well data sets, less suited data unequal group sizes. Method "sem" fits two-level structural equation model (via lavaan::sem()) estimates within-group -group covariance matrices simultaneously using maximum likelihood. Significance based resulting z-tests. groups weighted implicitly maximum likelihood estimation rather weight argument, method principled choice data unequal group sizes moderate amount missing data. slower "decomposition" can occasionally fail converge small collinear data sets. method = "sem", variables never vary within group (e.g., time-invariant traits) modeled -group level, variables almost -group variance (intraclass correlation near zero) modeled within-group level; corresponding cells unused level reported NA. Method "bayes" mirrors "decomposition", estimates correlations via Bayesian multivariate models fit brms::brm() (requires brms package) instead closed-form formulas, reporting posterior medians credible intervals (via ci) place point estimates p-values. requires folder argument cache fitted models, can take considerably longer two methods, useful number groups small communicating uncertainty via credible intervals priority. See vignette("correlation-methods") details number models fit caching behavior.

title: mlstats 0.1.0
text: CRAN release: 2026-07-11 Initial CRAN release. within_between_correlations() computes within-group -group correlations nested data (e.g., repeated measurements per person, students nested within schools), using one three methods: variance decomposition (default), two-level structural equation modeling (via lavaan), Bayesian multilevel modeling (via brms). mldesc() creates publication-ready descriptive statistics tables combine means, SDs, ranges, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), within-/-group correlations single table. decompose_within_between() decomposes variables within-group -group components use Random Effects Within-(REWB) models. Result tables print tibbles default can exported gt tinytable objects via print(result, format = "gt") print(result, format = "tt"). Includes media_diary example dataset, simulated daily-diary study used throughout documentation vignettes illustrate within-person vs. -person relationships.
